On October 21st, Meta reported its third-quarter earnings, the first since it launched its popular AI agent, Muse. Despite continued revenue growth, up 26% to $64.6 billion, Meta has been spending so heavily that free cash flow has gone negative. And that's unusual for Meta, a company known for printing cash.

<DashboardEmbed collection="meta-muse-wonder" slug="the-waterline" />

But could its ambitions in AI be so great that it's sinking the ship? That's not Mark Zuckerberg's perspective. By Zuck's numbers, Muse is one of Meta's most successful launches ever.

## Zuckerberg's Scorecard

Zuck opened up the earnings call with his broad view on the business. Meta has continued growing users, with 3.64 billion people using its apps every day and engagement at an all-time high. He also snuck in a huge insight: Threads has now passed X in monthly users, by Meta's count. That one really broke my brain, because I don't know anyone who uses Threads.

<DashboardEmbed collection="meta-muse-wonder" slug="the-scorecard" />

## All Eyes on Muse

But the reality is, all eyes were on Meta's AI agent and model family, Muse. So what exactly is Muse?

It's Meta's personal AI agent, which it launched on September 8th. Rather than just answering questions, it can open a browser, fill out forms and actually buy things for you, in its own app or right inside WhatsApp. On the call, Zuckerberg said:

> "In just a month and a half, more than 10 million people in the US and Canada have set up Muse personal agents. Growth continues to be strong and we have been #1 in the App Store almost every day. Engagement and retention are also off to a strong start. About 25% of people who have set up Muse use it on any given day."

That's roughly 2.5 million people using it on any given day, and Zuck says that rate is more than twice where Threads started. And the people using it look like Meta's best customers. More than a quarter of weekly users are shopping with it. Almost 30% have connected another app or service to it. And Meta said more than 20% of Muse's US users are worth $1,000 or more a year to the company.

It's still small in the context of Meta's business, well under 1% of the 3.6 billion people on its apps, and it's still only in the US and Canada. But for six weeks in, that's a genuinely impressive start. And some core use cases are already emerging:

> "The most common use case for Muse is shopping, with more than a quarter of people who are using Muse engaging in this, with an average purchase size of over $200. Plaid told us that they hadn't seen activity like they're seeing with their connector on any other service before, and in the first week, we had to work with Stripe to raise credit limits since the volumes were above what any of us expected."

So Muse is powering real transactions, but Meta isn't capturing any of that value yet. Meta said, "Today, we are not monetizing Muse outside of subscriptions." And Zuck reiterated that the goal is to build a large platform business over time, not to nickel and dime people to pay for the agent:

> "So, we'd like to create a large-scale Muse network as quickly as possible. ... For most people, the product should be free, and we will build commerce tools so we get paid a fee based on the transactions that we help facilitate. We expect this will be paid for by businesses."

But that only works if Meta can serve enough people, cheaply enough. And Muse is extremely compute-intensive, as Zuckerberg states:

> "On the compute side, we are building out the capacity to serve more than a billion people over the next few years. In the near term, Muse is very compute intensive to run, but we expect to improve its cost efficiency by more than 10x in the next year, which will enable it to be profitable once the revenue lines are at scale."

In other words, Zuck is building for a billion users before Muse makes much money, and betting that his agent will win big. But Muse is only as smart as the model running it.

## Muse Wonder

On October 12th, Meta launched Muse Wonder. It's Meta's first frontier model, meaning one built to compete with the very best AI models, and Meta trained it at Prometheus, its gigawatt-scale data center. So Zuckerberg is obviously bullish on Muse Wonder:

> "Muse Wonder is state of the art across many dimensions that matter for personal superintelligence. This validates the importance of training models ourselves to deliver the best experience."

Others online have said the model is benchmaxxed, or fitted to perform well on benchmarks. But one independent benchmarking firm, Artificial Analysis, was a little more measured, scoring Wonder's strongest version at 56, just behind Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 at 58.

<DashboardEmbed collection="meta-muse-wonder" slug="muse-wonder" />

For now, Wonder only powers Muse for people who pay. The free version runs on Muse Spark, a cheaper model. And Zuckerberg added:

> "We are also working on new smaller models that are coming out soon that will deliver Muse Wonder level intelligence more efficiently."

And in November, Muse comes to Meta's glasses. Reality Labs, the division behind them, lost about $4.1 billion this quarter, and Meta expects it to lose about $15 billion in 2027, down from as much as $19 billion in 2026.

But the agent, the models, and now the glasses all lean on Meta's data centers. And those are getting very expensive.

## The Bill

Luckily, Meta's core business is still printing money. Revenue was $64.6 billion, up 26% from a year ago, and almost all of it came from ads. Meta showed 10% more ads than a year ago and charged 14% more for each one. So the ad business is the cash cow, still healthy and keeping the trains running on time.

<DashboardEmbed collection="meta-muse-wonder" slug="the-revenue" />

But operating profit has seen a precipitous decline, down 37% to $13 billion. That was down to a $9.9 billion charge for settling teen mental health lawsuits. Even so, the cash coming in from Meta's business, or its operating cash flow, still grew 9%, to $32.8 billion.

<DashboardEmbed collection="meta-muse-wonder" slug="profit-and-cash" />

But what really caught analysts' attention was the free cash flow, or the cash that's left over once Meta pays for all of its investments, which went below zero. And the settlement isn't what took it there. It was capex, the money Meta spends on things like data centers. Meta spent $34.9 billion on capex this quarter alone, driving free cash flow into the red, to minus $2.1 billion. For perspective, just a year ago, free cash flow was over $10 billion for the quarter.

And by Meta's own numbers, it now holds a little more debt than cash: $83.7 billion of debt against $82.4 billion of cash and investments. Historically, that's a huge departure from the norm for Meta. For years, it produced tons of cash with room to spare. But in the AI era, that's flipped.

<DashboardEmbed collection="meta-muse-wonder" slug="cash-in-cash-out" />

And the spending is about to get a lot bigger. Meta expects to spend up to $145 billion on capex this year, an eye-watering number, roughly double the $72 billion it spent in 2025. With about $86 billion spent so far this year through September, that leaves about $50 to $60 billion for the fourth quarter alone.

<DashboardEmbed collection="meta-muse-wonder" slug="the-capex-column" />

Initially, markets reacted positively to the call, with Meta's stock rising in after-hours trading. But then it took a turn, and by the close on October 22nd, it was down almost 7%. The coverage tied it to the spending.

<DashboardEmbed collection="meta-muse-wonder" slug="the-stock" />

## A Theoretical Maximum

But Meta's other announcement that day is where things get really interesting. It's issuing a new class of stock with no vote, which lets Meta sell stock from January 2027 onward without touching Zuck's control, up to a point. And a filing on the new shares says management's forecasts showed "the Company's need to raise hundreds of billions of dollars over a period of several years beginning as early as fall 2026."

Now, Meta called that "a theoretical maximum," not its actual plan. But it still spooked many investors, who were already concerned seeing Meta ramp up capex to $145 billion for 2026.

<DashboardEmbed collection="meta-muse-wonder" slug="a-theoretical-maximum" />

As I was finishing this piece, on October 26th, Meta actually announced it's selling about $35 billion in new stock to pay for its AI build-out, and plans to set up a program to sell up to another $60 billion early in 2027.

<DashboardEmbed collection="meta-muse-wonder" slug="the-raise" />

The $35 billion comes in two parts: about $22.5 billion of regular Class A shares, and about $12.5 billion of preferred stock that has to convert into regular shares later. The $60 billion would be what's called an at-the-market program, which simply means Meta sells new shares into the market a little at a time, and it plans to start once the new non-voting shares begin trading.

So this went from a theoretical maximum to, it sounds like, an inevitability in 2027.

## What the Analysts Asked

Now, during the Q&A, analysts kept circling two main topics. One, what's slowing Muse down? And two, when will Muse start to pay for itself? One Morgan Stanley analyst asked Zuckerberg if there were any constraints on Muse's growth, and Zuckerberg had this to say:

> "One of the biggest constraints so far is that because this is a compute-intensive service to run, we have not launched it globally yet."

Shortly after, the question turned to how Meta will actually make money from Muse, and Zuckerberg said:

> "My guess, I think that we are going to work on monetization somewhat sooner on this than our normal playbook for a couple of reasons. One is just the size of the numbers that we're talking about in terms of both the costs and the opportunity, I think make it kind of important to make progress on that in order to be able to scale it."

Meta also mentioned that it wouldn't rule out advertising as a way to monetize Muse.

## Meta's AI Strategy

Ultimately, Zuck's goal is what he calls personal superintelligence, an AI agent for everybody. To get there, Meta ultimately believes it needs to train its own AI models, which is why it rebooted its AI lab in 2025 as Meta Superintelligence Labs. And Zuck tapped Alexandr Wang to lead it, though Wang himself wasn't mentioned by name once in any of these calls.

Meta would go on to outline four main ways it's thinking about making money from its AI models. The first is ads, and Meta says its AI is "already delivering substantial incremental advertising revenue." The second is subscriptions, which is the only way Muse makes money today. The third is pushing harder into the enterprise market with Muse, via the Meta Enterprise Platform. Zuckerberg explained why:

> "One other note on compute economics is that since training is a large fixed cost, now that we have leading models, we want to serve as much high margin inference demand as possible. That is why we are building the Meta Enterprise Platform, led by CJ Desai."

That enterprise business sells access to Meta's models, a coding tool called Muse Code at $5 to $200 a month, and AI agents for businesses. That puts Meta up against Anthropic, which has spent the last year winning over businesses with Claude, Claude Code and Cowork. But Meta has reach. It estimates at least 500 million small businesses already use its apps.

And Anthropic is also coming after Meta's business. The same day Meta reported, Anthropic opened an early preview of Claude Duet, its own proactive AI agent, to compete with the likes of Muse and Grok Bot.

The fourth way Meta is envisioning making money is via agentic commerce. This hasn't happened yet, but it's essentially Muse buying things on your behalf, with Meta eventually taking a cut of each transaction. Zuck is very bullish here, and Meta is writing an open standard with partners like Walmart, Stripe and Shopify, so your agent can deal directly with a store's agent.

<DashboardEmbed collection="meta-muse-wonder" slug="the-strategy" />

But Muse's revenue is still a long way behind its spending, so we ran some rough math of our own on what Muse could actually make in 2027. In our most generous case, 300 million people use it, 4% of them pay $20 a month, and almost a third shop through it twice a month, spending about $200 each time, with Meta taking a 3% cut. That comes to about $16 billion, around a tenth of Meta's capex this year alone.

<DashboardEmbed collection="meta-muse-wonder" slug="the-muse-cases" />

So ultimately, that business, even in the most optimistic case, is not going to be break-even or profitable anywhere in the near term. Zuck's answer to that gap is to lean in on the crown jewel, the ad business:

> "In the near term, the strength of our core business enables us to scale the Muse network before then, and we believe that we are the best positioned company to pursue this strategy."

## Sinking the Ship?

So is Meta sinking the ship? Not yet. It's still a growth company, with revenue up 26%. But the ad business now has to pay for everything else. And this quarter, for the first time in at least two years, Meta spent more than its business brought in.

<DashboardEmbed collection="meta-muse-wonder" slug="not-yet" />

Zuck's all in on AI. And how Muse does over the next few quarters could be make or break for the future of Meta's business.
